title: Understand Functions Core Test
description: Identify inputs, reason about unique outputs, and explain representations and counterexamples.

questions.questionText: A machine assigns input 11 to output 15. Under the same rule, can that same input also have output 16?
questions.correctAnswer: No; one input cannot have two different outputs.
questions.explanation: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Changing the output for the same input would violate that rule.
options: No; one input cannot have two different outputs.
Yes; functions allow any number of outputs per input.
Yes; both outputs are positive.
No; outputs must equal inputs.

questions.questionText: The complete relation is (11, 7), (12, 7), (13, 7). Is it a function of the first coordinate?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes; each input has one output.
questions.explanation: Different inputs may share an output. Check each first coordinate separately; none has conflicting outputs.
options: No; the output 7 repeats.
Yes; each input has one output.
No; a function must increase.
Yes; any three pairs form a function.

questions.questionText: The function rule is: add 5 to the input. What is the output for input 11?
questions.explanation: Apply the rule to the input: 11 + 5 = 16. The result is the output.

questions.questionText: A rule sends 11 to 20. Which number is the input?
questions.explanation: In an input-to-output statement, the starting number is the input. The number it is sent to is the output.

questions.questionText: The complete list is (11, 3), (11, 8). Which fact prevents it from being a function of x?
questions.correctAnswer: Input 11 has outputs 3 and 8.
questions.explanation: The conflict is two different outputs for one input. Different outputs at different inputs would be allowed.
options: There are only two pairs.
Input 11 has outputs 3 and 8.
The outputs are different numbers.
The numbers are all positive.

questions.questionText: A function already contains (11, 4) and (12, 6). Which new pair would create a conflict?
questions.explanation: The existing input 11 already has output 4. Assigning it 9 would give two outputs; the other options introduce new inputs.

questions.questionText: A relation records (11, 5), (11, 5), (12, 8). Does the repeated identical record break the function rule?
questions.correctAnswer: No; the repeated input still has only one distinct output.
questions.explanation: Recording the same pair twice adds no new assignment. A repeated input breaks the rule only when its outputs disagree.
options: No; the repeated input still has only one distinct output.
Yes; an input may never be recorded twice.
Yes; outputs must be unique.
No; duplicate inputs can have any outputs.

questions.questionText: A function doubles its input, then subtracts 3. Which input produces output 23?
questions.explanation: Work backward: add 3 to 23, then divide by 2. Check: 2(13) - 3 = 23.

questions.questionText: At a school with 21 students, each student is assigned exactly one homeroom. Several students share a room. Is student-to-homeroom a function?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes; each student has exactly one assigned room.
questions.explanation: Inputs and outputs need not be numbers. Shared outputs are allowed; the unique room assigned to each student is what matters.
options: No; a room cannot be shared.
No; the inputs are not numbers.
Yes; each student has exactly one assigned room.
Yes; every relation involving students is a function.

questions.questionText: A machine is tested at inputs 11, 12, and 13, with one output observed each time. What can you conclude about untested inputs?
questions.correctAnswer: The observations show no conflict, but do not prove the machine follows a function rule for every allowed input.
questions.explanation: A finite sample can reveal a violation, but cannot establish unspecified behavior outside that sample. A complete rule or specification is needed.
options: Every untested input must give the same output.
The observations show no conflict, but do not prove the machine follows a function rule for every allowed input.
Three tests prove the entire machine is a function.
The machine cannot be a function unless every output differs.

questions.questionText: A function sends 11 to 4 and 12 to 4. Reverse these assignments. Is the reverse relation a function of its input?
questions.correctAnswer: No; input 4 now has two different outputs.
questions.explanation: Reversing produces (4, 11) and (4, 12). The shared original output becomes one input with two outputs.
options: No; input 4 now has two different outputs.
Yes; reversing any function preserves the function rule.
No; reversing a relation removes all inputs.
Yes; the original inputs were different.

questions.questionText: For each real input x, a relation allows every y with y squared = x squared. At x = 11, what shows this is not a function of x?
questions.correctAnswer: Both y = 11 and y = -11 are allowed.
questions.explanation: Both 11 and -11 have square 121. Since this nonzero input has two allowed outputs, the relation fails the function rule.
options: Only y = 11 is allowed.
Only y = 0 is allowed.
There are no allowed outputs.
Both y = 11 and y = -11 are allowed.

questions.questionText: For whole-number inputs, a rule outputs x + 2 when x is even, and x - 1 when x is odd. Is this a function, and what is its output at 23?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes; the output is 22, using the odd-input rule.
questions.explanation: Every whole number is either even or odd, never both. Exactly one instruction applies to each input, so the rule assigns one output.
options: No; having two instructions always makes two outputs.
Yes; the output is 25, using the even-input rule.
No; odd inputs cannot belong to functions.
Yes; the output is 22, using the odd-input rule.

questions.questionText: A temperature app uses only the day number as input. On day 11, it reports 12 degrees at noon and 17 degrees at 3 p.m. Which change makes the input specific enough for one recorded output?
questions.correctAnswer: Use the pair (day, time) as the input, with one reading for each pair.
questions.explanation: The day alone does not distinguish the two readings. Including time makes the input identify the particular measurement.
options: Keep only the day as input and assign both outputs.
Use the pair (day, time) as the input, with one reading for each pair.
Replace both readings with their sum without changing the task.
Require different days to have different temperatures.
